## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ambajātaka* (Ja 124) is a narrative in the Pali Jātaka collection. According to its commentary, the Buddha delivered the teaching while residing at Jetavana with reference to a virtuous monk from a noble Sāvatthī brahmin family who proved constant in all his monastic duties [Fausböll 1877]. In the narrative of the past, a hermit demonstrates profound compassion during a famine by collecting water for suffering wild animals, neglecting his own hunger; moved by gratitude, the animals reciprocate by supplying him with an abundance of wild fruit [UNDV 2009]. Concluding the story, the Buddha identifies the dutiful hermit as the diligent monk of the present and reveals that he himself was then the leader of the hermit community (*gaṇasatthā*) [Fausböll 1877].
